item.title: [Marketing 101 #12] Why That Ad Found You Ten Seconds After You Searched
item.body:
> Digital marketing isn't one thing — it's three different jobs: social media goes where attention already is, search advertising catches demand at the exact moment someone types it, and content marketing earns trust long before anyone is ready to buy.

## Today's Concept

Most people picture "digital marketing" as a single blob of ads on the internet. It's more useful to think of it as three distinct jobs, each answering a different question about the customer.

**Social media marketing** answers: *how do we reach people who aren't looking for us yet?* On Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, LinkedIn, or Reddit, nobody opened the app to shop. They came for entertainment or connection. So the ad has to earn its place in the feed — it interrupts. That means you pay for **attention** and target by *who someone is* (age, location, interests, past behavior, lookalikes of your existing customers). Demand here is **latent**: you're creating want that wasn't there five seconds ago.

**Search advertising** answers: *how do we show up when someone is already looking?* Someone types "emergency plumber Chicago" into Google. They have a problem right now. You're not creating demand — you're **harvesting** it. That's why search clicks convert far better than social clicks, and why they cost more.

Here's the part most beginners get wrong: search ads are not a simple "highest bidder wins" auction. Google and Bing rank ads roughly by a combination of your bid and how relevant and useful your ad and landing page are (Google calls its relevance signal **Quality Score**). Simplified:

```
Ad Rank ≈ Max Bid × Quality Score (plus other context signals)
```

The practical consequence: a well-written ad pointing to a fast, relevant landing page can outrank a competitor who bids more. Relevance is a discount.

**Content marketing** answers: *how do we get chosen when someone finally compares options?* Blog posts, comparison guides, newsletters, YouTube explainers, podcasts. You're not selling — you're being useful. The payoff is slow and compounding: an article that ranks in search or gets shared keeps working for months or years after you publish it, with no per-click cost. The tradeoff is that it takes time to build and is hard to attribute cleanly.

A common way to organize all three is the **paid / owned / earned** framework:

- **Paid** — you rent the audience (social ads, search ads). Fast, measurable, stops the moment you stop paying.
- **Owned** — you control the asset (your website, blog, email list, app). Slow to build, but it's yours.
- **Earned** — others give it to you (word of mouth, press, reviews, shares). Most credible, least controllable.

Healthy programs use all three. Paid buys you speed; owned buys you independence from ad costs; earned buys you credibility neither of the others can purchase directly.

## In Everyday Life

Say you're in Denver and your knees have been hurting after runs.

**Tuesday night.** You're scrolling Instagram and a 15-second Reel from a shoe brand shows a runner explaining why flat feet need stability shoes. You weren't shopping. You watch it, don't click, and forget it. That's *social* — latent demand, paid for by impressions and attention.

**Saturday morning.** Your knees hurt again. You Google "best stability running shoes flat feet." The top two results say **Sponsored**. That's *search* — you expressed the demand, and brands paid to be there. A retailer's ad for local running stores might cost them somewhere in the range of a few dollars per click for a term like that, because the intent is worth it.

**Saturday afternoon.** Below the ads, you find a running store's guide: "How to Tell If You Overpronate — A 60-Second At-Home Test." No sales pitch, just a wet-footprint test. You trust these people now. That's *content* — the store paid a writer once, and that page has been earning attention ever since.

**Sunday.** An ad for that exact shoe follows you across a news site and Instagram. That's **retargeting** — the store's pixel recognized you as a past visitor. Creepy, effective, and legally constrained (and in California, opt-outs under CCPA/CPRA apply).

Now the business math, from the store's side. Suppose they spend **$600/month** on search ads at a **$3.00 average CPC**:

```
$600 ÷ $3.00 = 200 clicks
200 clicks × 4% conversion rate = 8 orders
$600 ÷ 8 orders = $75 CAC (customer acquisition cost)
```

If the average order is $120 and gross margin is 50%, each order contributes **$60** — less than the **$75** it cost to acquire. That campaign *loses money on the first purchase*. It only works if that runner comes back and buys again, which is exactly why the store also invests in an email list and useful content: to lift the **lifetime value (LTV)** above the acquisition cost. Digital marketing looks like a creative discipline, but it's decided on this arithmetic.

## 3-Line Recap

1. Social creates demand among people not yet looking; search harvests demand at the moment it's expressed; content builds trust that makes both cheaper over time.
2. Search ad position is bid **and** relevance — better ads and landing pages effectively lower your cost.
3. A campaign isn't "working" because clicks are cheap; it works when acquisition cost stays below the customer's lifetime value.

## ✅ Self Quiz

**1.** Which channel primarily *harvests* existing demand rather than creating it?
   A) Instagram Reels ads  B) Google search ads  C) A brand blog  D) A podcast sponsorship

**2. True or False:** In Google's ad auction, the advertiser with the highest bid always gets the top spot.

**3.** A store spends $1,000 on ads and gets 10 new customers, each with an average order of $80 and a 50% gross margin. On the *first* purchase alone, this campaign is:
   A) Profitable  B) Breaking even  C) Losing money  D) Impossible to evaluate

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **CPC (Cost Per Click)** — What you pay each time someone clicks your ad; the standard pricing model for search advertising.
- **CTR (Click-Through Rate)** — Clicks divided by impressions; a core measure of whether your ad actually appeals to the people seeing it.
- **Quality Score** — Google Ads' 1–10 diagnostic of expected click-through rate, ad relevance, and landing page experience; higher relevance can win better positions at a lower cost.
- **Retargeting (Remarketing)** — Showing ads specifically to people who already visited your site or app.
- **CAC / LTV** — Customer Acquisition Cost versus Lifetime Value; the ratio that determines whether growth is actually sustainable.
- **Paid / Owned / Earned Media** — Audiences you rent, channels you control, and attention others give you voluntarily.

---

*Answers: **1 — B.** Search ads reach people who have already typed a query, meaning the need exists before the ad appears. Social and content ads mostly reach people who weren't looking. **2 — False.** Ad rank combines bid with relevance signals like Quality Score, so a more relevant advertiser can outrank a higher bidder — and often pays less per click. **3 — C, losing money.** Each order contributes $40 in gross margin ($80 × 50%), so 10 customers contribute $400 against $1,000 spent — a $600 shortfall. It can still be a sound investment if those customers buy again, but only repeat purchases make it so.*
